title: The Omer: one quality a day
hookLine: the mystics pair each of the forty-nine days with a quality to refine

lines: A COUNTDOWN, OR A TRAINING PLAN?
cards: Every evening for seven weeks, after nightfall, observant Jews say a blessing and then a number. Today is one day of the Omer. Today is two days.

Today is eight days, which is one week and one day. Miss a whole day, and by many rulings you keep counting but stop saying the blessing. Apps, wall charts and little fridge calendars help people keep track.
It sounds like the world's most patient countdown. But the mystics turned these forty-nine days into something closer to a training plan.

teach.b: Start with the Torah. In Leviticus, from the day the first sheaf of barley is brought, the omer, you count. In the old Jewish translation: "seven weeks shall there be complete."
On the fiftieth day comes Shavuot, the feast of weeks.
In the rabbis' reading, it's the road from leaving Egypt to receiving the Torah at Sinai: freedom first, then what to do with it. The word for counting is sefirah, and here the mystics come in.
In the Kabbalah, a very similar word, sefirot, names the qualities through which God is revealed in the world.

The lower seven are usually listed as chesed, loving-kindness; gevurah, strength or restraint; tiferet, beauty and balance; netzach, endurance; hod, humility or splendor; yesod, foundation, the bond between people; and malchut, kingship, presence, the way it all shows up in the world.
Seven qualities, seven weeks, and inside each week, seven days. So the first day is loving-kindness within loving-kindness. The second, strength within loving-kindness: love that knows its limits.

Forty-nine combinations, one each night. Kabbalists and Hasidic teachers built a practice on it, and many teachers of character, middot, still use it: each day, look at one quality in yourself and refine it a little.
Just today's square on the chart.
The counting stops being a wait and becomes the preparation. By the time you reach the mountain, you've worked on the person who's arriving.

how: From the second night of Passover until Shavuot, observant Jews count the Omer each evening with a blessing, naming the day and week; many also follow the Kabbalistic chart of sefirot, reflecting on one quality each day.

games.q: it's the second day of the first week of the Omer. on the mystics' chart, which quality are you working on?
games.why: strength within loving-kindness: love that knows its limits. the first week is loving-kindness; the second day adds strength.

practice: Choose one quality: kindness, restraint, balance, endurance, humility, connection or presence, maybe the one that's been weakest lately, or too strong.
Think of one moment today when it'll be tested, a meeting, a dinner, a drive, and picture meeting it with that quality a little more refined. Just a little.
